hero.title: Build vs. Buy AI: The 2025 Decision Framework
hero.highlightedText: Build when it differentiates. Buy when it's utility.
hero.description: Build custom AI when your use case requires domain-specific accuracy that generic platforms can't achieve, deep integration with proprietary systems, data privacy requirements preventing shared cloud AI infrastructure, or competitive differentiation. Buy SaaS AI platforms when your use case is generic, speed to market matters more than optimization, and your differentiation lies elsewhere.

sections.title: Build or buy? A simple filter for a complex decision
sections.description: Before diving into detailed criteria, use this decision filter to identify which direction is likely right for your situation.

items.title: Strong signal to BUILD custom
items.description: Your AI needs to be trained on your proprietary data to be accurate. You need AI that competitors can't access by subscribing to the same platform. Vendor platforms have tried and failed on your use case. Your industry has data privacy requirements preventing external API use. AI is a core differentiator — not a supporting tool — in your product.
items.label: Build

items.title: Strong signal to BUY (SaaS platform)
items.description: Your use case is generic (content writing, meeting transcription, basic Q&A). You need a solution in 2–4 weeks, not 3–6 months. The AI is a utility function, not a differentiator. Vendor platforms cover 90%+ of your requirements without customization. Your data can safely reside on vendor infrastructure.
items.label: Buy

sections.title: 7 scenarios where custom AI development beats buying
sections.description: Custom development is the right choice when accuracy, differentiation, integration depth, or data control matter more than speed.

blocks.heading: 1. Domain-Specific Accuracy Requirements
paragraphs: Generic AI models perform well on general language and common tasks. They underperform on specialized domain content: clinical notes, legal contracts, financial instruments, specialized industrial processes, proprietary product catalogs. If accuracy on your specific domain content determines whether the AI is useful, you need a model trained on your domain data — which means building.

**Real example:** A healthcare documentation SaaS tried four commercial transcription services before building a custom clinical vocabulary model that achieved the necessary medical terminology accuracy.

blocks.heading: 2. Proprietary Data as a Moat
paragraphs: If your competitive advantage is unique proprietary data, building AI that's trained on that data creates a competitive moat that buying a vendor platform cannot. When you buy a vendor AI product, every competitor can access the same capability by subscribing to the same service.

blocks.heading: 3. Deep System Integration Requirements
paragraphs: Vendor AI platforms are designed for common system integrations (Salesforce, Zendesk, Slack, Google Workspace). If your use case requires deep integration with proprietary legacy systems, specialized industry platforms, or unusual data architectures that vendor connectors don't support, custom development is often more practical than building extensive custom middleware.

blocks.heading: 4. Data Privacy and Residency Requirements
paragraphs: HIPAA, financial services data residency requirements, classified data constraints, and EU data residency requirements can prevent sending data to vendor AI APIs. Self-hosted custom AI (open-source models like Llama 3 and Mistral deployed on your infrastructure) is the only viable option when external API transmission isn't permitted.

blocks.heading: 5. Cost at Scale
paragraphs: At low volume, vendor AI API costs are negligible. At high volume — millions of API calls per month — the math changes. A self-hosted Llama 3 70B inference cluster typically breaks even against GPT-4o API costs at approximately 5–10 million monthly API calls, depending on model size and prompt length. High-volume applications eventually benefit from owning the inference infrastructure.

blocks.heading: 6. Output Quality That Matters Commercially
paragraphs: For customer-facing AI features that directly affect product quality perception, vendor model quality may be insufficient or inconsistently aligned with your brand voice. Custom fine-tuning on your content and brand standards produces more consistently on-brand outputs than generic models.

blocks.heading: 7. Regulatory Documentation Requirements
paragraphs: SR 26-2 model risk management (US banking), FDA Software as a Medical Device documentation (healthcare AI), and EU AI Act technical documentation (high-risk AI systems) require documentation of model architecture, training data, validation methodology, and ongoing monitoring. Vendor platforms typically don't provide this level of technical documentation.

sections.title: 5 scenarios where buying a SaaS AI platform is the right move
sections.description: Buying is the right choice for generic use cases, speed-to-market priorities, and when you lack ML engineering capacity for ongoing maintenance.

blocks.heading: 1. Generic Use Cases with Strong Vendor Coverage
paragraphs: Content drafting assistance, meeting transcription, email summarization, general translation, and grammar checking — these are genuinely well-served by vendor products (GPT-4, Claude, Grammarly, Otter.ai). Building custom for generic use cases wastes development budget that could fund differentiated custom AI elsewhere.

blocks.heading: 2. Speed to Market Is Critical
paragraphs: Vendor AI products deploy in days to weeks; custom development takes months. If market timing is critical and the AI capability doesn't need to be differentiated, buying buys time.

blocks.heading: 3. Your Team Will Not Maintain Custom AI
paragraphs: Custom AI requires ongoing maintenance: model retraining, drift monitoring, infrastructure management. If your organization doesn't have the ML engineering capacity to maintain custom AI post-deployment, vendor-managed infrastructure avoids creating a technical liability.

blocks.heading: 4. Buying Validates the Use Case Before Building
paragraphs: For unproven use cases, buying a vendor product proves whether users actually adopt and value the AI capability before investing in custom development. If users don't engage with the vendor product, the custom development investment would have been wasted.

blocks.heading: 5. The Use Case Evolves With Vendor Improvements
paragraphs: Vendor foundation models improve significantly with each release — a capability that's mediocre today may be excellent in 6 months as the underlying model improves. Custom-built models don't automatically benefit from these improvements.

sections.title: Buy then build: the most cost-effective path for many organizations
sections.description: Start with vendor AI to validate the use case, then build custom for the specific components where vendor limitations become bottlenecks.

blocks.heading: Sequence the investment efficiently
paragraphs: **Phase 1 (Weeks 1–8):** Deploy vendor AI (OpenAI, Anthropic) to validate user adoption and identify capability gaps.
**Phase 2 (Months 3–6):** Build custom components where vendor accuracy or integration falls short.
**Phase 3 (Year 2):** Evaluate self-hosting at scale for cost optimization.

blocks.heading: Why this works
paragraphs: This approach minimizes risk — you're not committing to a large custom build before validating that users actually want the capability. And you're not stuck with vendor limitations forever — you build exactly what's needed where vendor products fall short.

sections.title: Questions about the build vs. buy AI decision
sections.description: Clear strategic and commercial answers before you commit to either path.

items.question: Can we start with a vendor AI product and switch to custom later?
items.answer: Yes — the hybrid approach is common. Starting with vendor products validates the use case; custom development captures value where vendor limitations become clear.

items.question: Is custom AI always more accurate than vendor AI for specialized domains?
items.answer: For specialized domain content (clinical notes, legal contracts, specialized industrial processes), custom fine-tuned models consistently outperform general vendor models when training data is adequate.

items.question: How long does the build-vs-buy decision process take?
items.answer: ClickMasters' Build vs. Buy assessment runs 2–4 weeks and includes vendor product evaluation alongside custom development feasibility.

items.question: What's the minimum volume that justifies self-hosting over API calls?
items.answer: Approximately 3–10 million monthly API calls, depending on the model size being self-hosted vs. the vendor model cost. ClickMasters models this specifically for your usage patterns.

items.question: Can ClickMasters help with both the build and the buy decision?
items.answer: Yes — ClickMasters evaluates vendor products honestly during the assessment, recommending the right approach for your situation rather than defaulting to custom development regardless of fit.

items.question: What's the risk of choosing the wrong approach?
items.answer: Building when you should buy: 3–6 months delayed and $50,000–$200,000 invested when a vendor product would have sufficed. Buying when you should build: ongoing accuracy problems, integration limitations, competitive commoditization, and eventual rebuild cost. ClickMasters' assessment de-risks both errors.
